questions.topic: Management account method: ONWC, NIC, NFP and an operating ROIC
questions.syllabus_objective: Reclassifying financial statements: management account method, operating vs financial vs non-operating items, NFP
questions.stem: Gamma SpA's balance sheet (€k) is below. Equity is the balancing item.
questions.data:
| Assets | €k |
|---|---|
| Property, plant and equipment | 820 |
| Right-of-use assets (leases) | 90 |
| Real estate held for investment (not used in operations) | 150 |
| Inventories | 210 |
| Trade receivables | 260 |
| Operating prepayments | 20 |
| Short-term loan to a related party | 40 |
| Marketable securities | 35 |
| Cash and cash equivalents | 75 |
| Deferred tax assets | 15 |

| Liabilities and equity | €k |
|---|---|
| Long-term bank loan | 380 |
| Lease liabilities | 95 |
| Current portion of long-term debt | 60 |
| Short-term bank debt | 50 |
| Trade payables | 240 |
| Accrued operating expenses | 45 |
| Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) | 30 |
| Income tax payable | 25 |
| Pension liabilities | 60 |
| Equity | 730 |

source.location: Lectures 3–4: management account method, NIC, NFP, ONWC and its borderline cases
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Using the management account method, compute Operating NWC, Net Invested Capital (asset side) and the Net Financial Position.

EBIT of €190k includes €12k of rent earned on the investment property. Compute ROIC on an operating basis (NOPAT at a 24% tax rate over NIC), and the ROIC an analyst would report by mixing in the property and its rent.

error_tags.trap: a: right-of-use assets left out of NIC
a: non-operating real estate included
a: NFP without lease liabilities (340)
a: loan to a related party treated as operating
b: non-operating rent kept in EBIT
b: EBIT not taxed

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) operating current assets = inventories 210 + receivables 260 + prepayments 20 = 490; (2) operating current liabilities = payables 240 + accrued 45 + customer prepayments 30 = 315; (3) ONWC = 175; (4) operating non-current = PP&E 820 + right-of-use 90 = 910 (investment property excluded); (5) NIC = 1085; (6) gross debt = 380 + 95 + 60 + 50 = 585 (leases included); (7) financial assets = cash 75 + securities 35 + related-party loan 40 = 150; (8) NFP = 435.
Second route for [a]: financing side 585 + 730 − 150 − investment property 150 = 1015; add back the items outside both NIC and NFP (pensions 60 + tax payable 25 − deferred tax assets 15 = 70) → 1085.

[b] Steps: (1) operating EBIT = 190 − 12 = 178; (2) NOPAT = 178 × 0.76 = 135.28; (3) ROIC = 135.28/1085 = 12.47%; (4) mixed version = 190 × 0.76 / (1085 + 150) = 11.69%; (5) the property drags the ratio down: it earns 12 on 150, well below the core business.

Where marks are lost: leaving out right-of-use assets, putting investment property in NIC, leaving leases out of NFP, treating the related-party loan or tax payable as operating, keeping the rent in operating EBIT.

citations.quote: Operating Net Working Capital = Operating Current Assets – Operating Short-term Liabilities
Non operating fixed assets are excluded from NIC.

citations.slide: Focus on the ONWC: borderline cases
citations.quote: Short-term financial receivables (eg. loans to related parties): exclude (financial).
it must be compared only against operational earnings (EBIT or NOPAT)

questions.topic: Liquidity view, value added and an outsourcing decision
questions.syllabus_objective: Reclassifying: liquidity-based balance sheet (financial NWC, treasury margin) and the value added income statement
questions.stem: Delta SpA (€k). Short-term assets: cash 40, short-term investments 30, trade receivables 180, inventories 150. Short-term liabilities: trade payables 170, short-term bank debt 90, current tax payable 20, accrued expenses 30. Income statement: revenues 2,000; increase in finished-goods inventory 50; capitalised internal work 30; raw materials 900; services 350; rents 60; personnel 420; D&A 110; interest 25.

source.location: Lectures 3–4: liquidity-based balance sheet; value added income statement
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Compute Financial NWC, the treasury margin, and the current and quick ratios, and say what the treasury margin tells you.

Compute the Value of Production, Value Added and the Value Added ratio. Then Delta outsources assembly: services rise by €150k and personnel costs fall by €120k. What happens to the VA ratio and to EBITDA?

answer_key.answer: Financial NWC 90; treasury margin -60; current ratio 1.29; quick ratio 0.81. Cash and receivables do not cover short-term liabilities: the company relies on selling inventory or on bank credit.
VoP 2080; VA 770; VA ratio 37.0%; after outsourcing VA 620, ratio 29.8%, EBITDA 350 → 320 (−30).

error_tags.trap: a: treasury margin computed like NWC
a: calls a positive NWC distress
b: inventory change and capitalised work left out
b: personnel deducted before Value Added

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) short-term assets = 400; (2) short-term liabilities = 310; (3) Financial NWC = 90; (4) treasury margin = 400 − 150 − 310 = -60; (5) current ratio = 1.29; (6) quick ratio = 250/310 = 0.81; (7) a negative treasury margin with positive NWC means the company must sell inventory or borrow to meet near-term payments.

[b] Steps: (1) VoP = 2,000 + 50 + 30 = 2080; (2) external costs = 900 + 350 + 60 = 1310; (3) VA = 770; (4) VA ratio = 770/2080 = 37.0%; (5) EBITDA = 770 − personnel 420 = 350; (6) outsourcing: external costs +150 → VA = 620; (7) ratio 29.8%: less vertical integration; (8) EBITDA = 620 − 300 = 320, down 30.

Where marks are lost: leaving inventories in the treasury margin, using revenues as value of production, deducting personnel before value added, or reading a lower VA ratio as lower efficiency by itself.
Not needed: D&A and interest (below EBITDA).

citations.quote: Treasury margin = short-term assets – inventories – short-term liabilities
Value Added Ratio = Value Added / Value of Production

citations.slide: Liquidity-based Balance Sheet: how do we interpret the values?
citations.quote: the company is forced to rely on future sales or bank credit to meet near-term payments

questions.topic: Indirect cash flow, the cash reconciliation and the equity roll-forward
questions.syllabus_objective: Accounting basics: cash flow statement (indirect method), reconciliation of cash, interrelation of the statements
questions.stem: Omicron SpA, 2026 (€m): net income 120; depreciation and amortisation 45; increase in provisions 10; gain on disposal of equipment 8 (proceeds €20m); receivables rose by 30; inventories fell by 12; trade payables rose by 18; capital expenditure 140. Revenues were 1,450 and the tax rate is 24%.

source.location: Session 2: cash flow statement (indirect method), reconciliation of cash, statement of shareholders' equity
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Prepare Omicron's cash flow from operating activities (indirect method) and from investing activities.

Opening cash was €60m and closing cash €70m. Omicron issued €40m of new debt, repaid €25m and paid dividends; there were no other financing flows. How much did it pay in dividends, and what is its closing equity if opening equity was €500m and OCI was −€6m?

error_tags.trap: a: disposal gain left in CFO
a: receivables increase added
a: proceeds counted in operations
b: CFF set to zero
b: closing equity without OCI

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) start from net income 120; (2) + D&A 45; (3) + increase in provisions 10; (4) − gain on disposal 8 (non-cash; the cash is in investing); (5) − receivables increase 30; (6) + inventory decrease 12; (7) + payables increase 18; CFO = 167. CFI = −140 + 20 = -120.
Check: 167 + (-120) + (-37) = +10 = change in cash.
Where marks are lost: leaving the disposal gain in CFO, reversing working-capital signs, putting disposal proceeds in operations, forgetting OCI.
Not needed: revenues and the tax rate (extraneous).

citations.quote: derives operating cash flow from profit or loss by adjusting for non-cash items, accruals and changes in operating working capital
Ending equity = Beginning equity + Profit or loss + Other comprehensive income + Owner contributions − Distributions to owners ± Other recognised equity movements

citations.slide: The Cash Flow Statement: Reconciliation of Cash
citations.quote: If the CFI (typically negative) exceeds the CFO, the deficit can be covered by either borrowing (through CFF) or using existing cash at hand

questions.topic: Accrual and deferral corrections, then the market premium
questions.syllabus_objective: Accounting basics: accrued and deferred revenues and expenses, contract liabilities, market vs book value of equity
questions.stem: An analyst reviews Rho SpA's 2026 accounts (reported net income €90m, tax rate 25%) and finds: (1) €30m of December delivery expenses were incurred but not recorded; (2) €25m of gift cards sold during the year were all recognised as revenue at sale, but only €10m had been redeemed by year end (ignore breakage); (3) a €12m insurance premium paid on 1 October 2026 for the following 12 months was fully expensed.

source.location: Session 2: accounting distortions, accrued and deferred items, equity at book vs market
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Correct Rho's 2026 net income for the three findings.
Rho has 50 million shares at €22.00 and reported book equity of €800m. Compute the market premium before and after the corrections.

answer_key.answer: Pre-tax effect -36; after tax -27.00; corrected net income 63.00 (€m).

error_tags.trap: a: all 25 of gift-card revenue reversed
a: the whole 12 added back
a: adjustments not tax-effected
b: calls the premium unrecognised goodwill

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) accrue delivery expenses: −30; (2) gift cards: revenue only on redemption, so defer 25 − 10 = 15: −15; (3) prepaid insurance: only 3 months (3) belong to 2026, so 9 is a prepaid asset: +9; (4) net pre-tax -36; (5) after 25% tax -27.00; (6) corrected NI = 63.00.

[b] Steps: (1) market value of equity = 50 × 22 = 1100; (2) premium on reported book = 1100 − 800 = 300; (3) corrected book equity = 800 − 27.00 = 773.00; (4) premium = 327.00. The premium reflects unrecognised intangibles, growth and expectations, not goodwill.
Where marks are lost: reversing all gift-card revenue, adding back all of the insurance, forgetting the tax effect, calling the premium goodwill.

citations.quote: When a gift card is sold, the consideration received is generally recognised as a contract liability.

citations.slide: Accounting distortions: accrued and deferred revenues and expenses
citations.quote: The company has incurred an expense but the cash will be paid in the next period.
Market premium = Market Value of Equity – Book Value of Equity

questions.topic: Connected player transfers and a founder's company without a price
questions.syllabus_objective: Why financial statements matter: transaction timing and recognition, price vs value, multiples as a starting point
questions.stem: Use the lecture's cases. Juventus bought Douglas Luiz for €50m (paid over four financial years) on 30 June 2024, capitalised the cost and signed him to 30 June 2029; amortise straight-line over the contract from 1 July 2024. On 1 July 2024 it sold Iling-Junior for €14m and Barrenechea for €8m, booking gains of €11.9m and €5.5m in 2024/25. Juventus's financial year ends on 30 June.

subquestions.prompt: From Juventus's side: compute the carrying amounts of the two players sold, the net cash committed across the three deals, and the net effect of the three deals on Juventus's 2024/25 operating result.

For Armani (2024 revenue €2.3bn, EBITDA €398m, EBIT €67m), compute the enterprise values implied by the four sector multiples, the resulting range, and the EV/EBITDA multiples implied by the published €6.5–10bn estimates.

answer_key.answer: Carrying amounts 2.1 and 2.5; net cash committed €28m; 2024/25 effect +7.4 (gains 17.4 − amortisation 10.0).

EVs: EV/EBITDA average 11.1× 4,417.8, EV/EBITDA median 9.7× 3,860.6, EV/Revenue average 2.7× 6,210.0, EV/Revenue median 1.6× 3,680.0; range €3.68–6.21bn; published estimates imply 16.3× to 25.1× EBITDA.

error_tags.trap: a: cost spread over the four payment years (12.5 a year)
a: sale prices counted as gains
b: EBIT used with an EBITDA multiple
b: range taken from the two averages only

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) Iling-Junior carrying amount = 14 − 11.9 = 2.1; (2) Barrenechea = 8 − 5.5 = 2.5; (3) net cash committed = 50 − 14 − 8 = 28; (4) amortisation of Luiz = 50 / 5 contract years = 10.0 a year (the four-year payment schedule is irrelevant to amortisation); (5) gains = 17.4; (6) 2024/25 effect = 17.4 − 10.0 = +7.4.
Where marks are lost: amortising over the payment period, counting sale prices as gains, applying multiples to EBIT, or quoting only the averages.
Not needed: EBIT of €67m (extraneous for these multiples).
